ai.title: Refactor runTerminalCommand to split PTY and child process
ai.summary: Refactored `runTerminalCommand` in `npm-app/src/utils/terminal.ts` by extracting PTY and child_process execution paths into separate `runCommandPty` and `runCommandChildProcess` functions. The main function now acts as a dispatcher based on `persistentProcess.type`. `MAX_EXECUTION_TIME` was moved to module scope to be shared by both implementations.

eli5.text: The terminal that runs your commands was rewritten to handle two different ways of executing commands separately, so it can better manage long-running processes and timeouts. Both the interactive shell (PTY) and the fallback command runner (child_process) now have their own dedicated code paths, and they share a common 30-second timeout limit that was previously buried inside one function. If you use the assistant to run shell commands, you may notice that Ctrl+C now more reliably stops a running command, and the shell is less likely to get stuck when a command takes too long. This is a behind-the-scenes refactor that improves stability and makes the code easier to maintain, but the overall experience of running commands remains the same for you today.

ai.title: CLI Ctrl+C now kills running terminal commands
ai.summary: CLI SIGINT handler now calls resetShell() to terminate active terminal processes before stopping response generation. Terminal utilities refactored from createPty to createPersistentProcess, adding isCommandRunning state tracking and explicit timer cleanup in resetShell. Double-SIGINT exit window extended from 3 to 5 seconds in cli.ts. Covers npm-app/src/cli.ts, npm-app/src/index.ts, and npm-app/src/utils/terminal.ts.

eli5.text: If you press Ctrl+C while a command is running in the terminal, it will now actually stop that command instead of just stopping the assistant. The time window to press Ctrl+C twice to fully exit has been extended from 3 to 5 seconds. This makes interrupting long-running terminal operations more reliable.

ai.title: Clear readline buffer on Ctrl-C
ai.summary: Ctrl-C handling in `npm-app/src/cli.ts` now explicitly clears the internal `readline` line buffer (`this.rl.line = ''`) before processing stop/response logic. This prevents stale input text from persisting in the terminal UI after an interrupt. Scope limited to CLI interface layer. Relies on internal `readline` API property access.

eli5.text: When you press Ctrl-C to interrupt what the program is doing, it now clears any half-typed command text from the input line before handling the stop. This affects the command-line interface used by the npm app, so if you were typing something and hit Ctrl-C, the leftover text won't linger or cause confusion in the terminal. You'd notice a cleaner interruption with no stale input remaining.

ai.title: Version bump to 1.0.149
ai.summary: Version bumped to 1.0.149. Internal release for npm-app package. Update package.json version field.

eli5.text: Today's update lets the assistant cleanly stop a running task when you press Ctrl+C. Previously, pressing Ctrl+C could leave background work still active or leave the command line in a messy state, but now it terminates the active work and clears the input buffer so you can safely start fresh. This is a behind-the-scenes version-label change that bundles several smaller recent fixes together.

ai.title: Strengthen git push prohibition in system prompt
ai.summary: Updated backend/src/system-prompt.ts to explicitly prohibit git push due to production breakage risk. Consolidated file modification and global installation warnings into a single rule requiring explicit permission. Adjusted guidance to instruct users to manually run long-running commands instead of attempting them.

eli5.text: The assistant has been told to never run the command that publishes your code changes to the shared repository, because doing that by accident can break things in production. The rules about which commands need your okay before running have also been simplified, and the assistant now asks you to run long-running tasks yourself instead of trying to do them. These are changes to how the assistant decides what actions are safe to take on your behalf.
